citations.title: Synthetic Data Generation Using Large Language Models
excerpts: Large language models (LLMs) have unlocked new possibilities for generating synthetic training data in both natural language and code domains. By producing artificial but task-relevant examples, these models can significantly augment or even substitute for real-world datasets, particularly in scenarios where labeled data is scarce, expensive, or sensitive. This paper surveys recent advances in leveraging LLMs to create synthetic text and code, highlighting key techniques such as prompt-based generation, retrieval-augmented pipelines, and iterative self-refinement. We examine how these methods can enrich low-resource tasks (e.g. classification, question answering) and facilitate code-centric applications (e.g. instruction tuning, code translation, bug repair) through automated verification of functional correctness.

Alongside potential benefits—cost-effectiveness, broad coverage, and controllable diversity—we discuss the accompanying challenges, including factual inaccuracies in generated text, insufficient stylistic or distributional realism, and risks of bias amplification. Proposed mitigation strategies range from filtering and weighting synthetic outputs to reinforcement learning with execution feedback in code domains. We conclude by outlining open research directions, such as automated prompt engineering, cross-modal data synthesis, and robust evaluation frameworks, underscoring the growing importance of LLM-generated synthetic data in accelerating AI development while emphasizing ethical and quality safeguards.

Distribution Alignment Another subtle issue is aligning the synthetic data distribution with the real data distribution of the task. Synthetic data that is too out-of-distribution may not actually help the model perform better on real data. For example, an LLM might generate very pedantic or overly complex sentences that, while correct, do not resemble the style of text the model will see at test time. Techniques like the Step-by-Step method mentioned earlier explicitly target alignment by focusing on misclassified real examples [ [49](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.14023v1.bib49) ] . Additionally, some works (e.g., [ [63](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.14023v1.bib63) ] in the context of topic-guided generation) aim to ensure the synthetic data covers the same topical space as the real data.

Post-Processing and Filtering -
After generation, it is common to apply filters or selection criteria to remove low-quality synthetic data. Simple heuristics include removing exact duplicates, checking for prompt leakage (e.g., the LLM copying the input example in a few-shot prompt verbatim), or enforcing output format correctness [ [61](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.14023v1.bib61) ] . More advanced techniques train a critic or classifier to judge the quality of synthetic examples [ [11](https://arxiv.org/html/2503.14023v1.bib11) ] . For instance, one could train a classifier to distinguish real vs. synthetic data and then drop synthetic examples that are too easily identified as fake (assuming those are less realistic).

# Triangulating P&C Claims Data: Grounding Jungl3's Synthetic Environment in Empirical Reality

## Executive Summary

To prevent plausibility collapse in Jungl3's v1 P&C claims environment, synthetic data generation must be anchored in reconciled empirical benchmarks. Analysis of statutory filings and vendor data reveals stark operational realities: property claims now average 44 days to close [1], auto total loss frequencies have hit a record 23.1% [2], and up to 51% of homeowner claims close without payment [3]. Furthermore, a "lived-in" auto claim requires a median of 21 distinct communications [4]. Because vendor data (e.g., CCC, Verisk) inherently skews toward severe or litigated claims, Jungl3 must reconcile these operational metrics against NAIC statutory baselines to maintain realistic overall frequencies and cost ceilings under ADR 0007.

## Source Inventory & Reconciliation Methodology

### Balancing statutory truth against vendor severity bias

To generate defendable parameters, we must reconcile conflicting data sources. Statutory data provides the ground truth for macro frequencies, while vendor data provides the micro-operational texture required for plausibility. 

| Source Category | Key Providers | Usage in Jungl3 v1 | Access/Data Quality Constraints |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Statutory/Regulatory** | NAIC Auto Database [5], State DOIs | Baseline claim frequencies, macro outcome mixes. | High credibility, but lags by 1-2 years. Lacks operational workflow granularity. |
| **Claims Processing Vendors** | CCC Intelligent Solutions [2], Verisk [6] | Auto total loss rates, repair cycle times, property severity. | Skews severe. Vendors see claims that require their software; minor/fast-track claims are underrepresented. |
| **Workflow/Communication** | Five Sigma [4], OpsDog [7] | Artifact density (emails, notes), stage dwell times. | Highly actionable for UI realism, but represents specific customer bases rather than industry averages. |
| **Fraud/SIU** | Shift Technology [8], Coalition Against Fraud [9] | SIU referral rates, automated trigger percentages. | High credibility for anomaly rates, but definitions of "referral" vary by carrier. |
| **Consumer Satisfaction** | J.D. Power [1], Weiss Ratings [3] | End-to-end cycle times, zero-payment closure rates. | Survey-based or aggregated; excellent for identifying worst-case bottlenecks. |

**Reconciliation Method:** 
1. **Weights:** Weight NAIC data at 80% for top-level arrival frequencies. Weight vendor data (CCC, Five Sigma) at 90% for artifact density and cycle times.
2. **Recency:** Prioritize 2024-2026 data to capture post-pandemic supply chain inflation and rising litigation trends [10].
3. **Data Quality Warning:** Data regarding "partial denials" and "reopened claims" is notoriously weak across all sources, as carriers classify these differently. Jungl3 should use conservative point estimates for these edge cases.

## Defendable Claim Frequencies & Arrival Parameters

### NAIC baselines dictate 5.2% auto collision and 1.6% property water frequencies

Cycle times have elongated significantly. J.D. Power reports an average of 44 days from FNOL to final payment for property claims [1]. Auto claims are also delayed due to repair complexity and parts shortages [10].
